title: GraphQL Errors: Partial Responses, Paths, Codes & Non-Null Propagation
summary: A 10-page study series on how GraphQL reports failure: the data + errors envelope, partial responses, error paths and extensions.code, the resolver error lifecycle, non-null propagation, masking internal errors, client-side handling, and the trade-offs versus REST-style signaling.

chapters.title: The Response Envelope: data + errors
points: A GraphQL response is one JSON object with at most three top-level keys: data, errors, extensions — application failures do not change the HTTP status.
data and errors can coexist: a 200 response may carry partial data plus error objects — partial success is the default contract, not an exception.
Each errors[] entry is a GraphQLError: message is the only spec-required field; locations, path, extensions are optional convention.
The spec defines NO error codes — everything beyond message is server convention, which is why extensions.code became the de facto standard.
Parse and validation errors happen before execution: the response is errors only, with data omitted entirely.
Execution errors happen per-resolver: the response is data (possibly partial) plus errors — always know which phase an error came from.
extensions is also a reserved top-level map for request-level metadata: tracing, cost, persisted-query info, requestId.
Worked example: user.name resolves, user.email throws — data.user.name is populated, user.email is null, errors[] holds one entry.
Servers may add unknown keys anywhere; clients must tolerate extra fields for forward compatibility.
Why this design: GraphQL operates on graphs — one broken leaf should not abort the whole tree, unlike a single REST resource.
Mental model: HTTP status = did transport work; errors[] = did execution work.
Antipattern preview: returning failures as data (user: { error: ... }) hides them from tooling and monitoring — real failures belong in errors[].

chapters.title: Partial Responses: One Broken Leaf Doesn't Kill the Tree
points: Definition: a partial response contains every successfully resolved field plus one errors[] entry per failed field.
Mechanics: resolvers run independently — a throw in one resolver is caught by the executor and never aborts sibling resolvers.
Executor rule on a field error: append a GraphQLError, set that field's value to null, continue executing the rest of the selection set.
The failed field shows up as null in data — that null is the hole the matching error path points at.
Multiple failures produce multiple errors[] entries, each with its own path; resolver completion order does not matter.
Lists fail per item: path posts[2].title means only post index 2's title failed, not the whole list.
Partial responses depend on nullable fields — non-null types change this behavior entirely (non-null propagation chapter).
Client contract: always null-check nested objects even on success; null + errors entry means a failed field, not missing data.
Example: feed of 10 posts, one author lookup fails — render 9 posts fully and a degraded card for the broken one.
REST contrast: a 500 on /feed kills the entire payload; GraphQL degrades field by field.
Trade-off: resilience buys ambiguity — clients must join data with errors[] to know what to trust.
Schema design rule: keep a field nullable when failure is recoverable at that node; reserve ! for when null makes the parent meaningless.

chapters.title: path & locations: Pinpointing Failures
points: errors[].path is an ordered array of field names and list indices from the response root down to the failing field.
Example: path user.friends[3].avatar = the 4th element of friends failed while resolving its avatar.
Paths use response keys: aliased fields appear under their alias, so path always matches the keys actually present in data.
errors[].locations gives {line, column} of the failing field in the query source text — great for dev tooling, rarely used at runtime.
No path = request-level error (parse/validation): the whole operation failed, so retry and refresh logic must differ from field errors.
Client recovery pattern: map each error.path to the UI component that owns that fragment — disable the broken widget, keep the rest.
Path is response-space: you never need to re-walk the query document or resolve fragments to find the failing node.
A resolver fanning out over a large list can emit many near-identical errors differing only in index — aggregate server-side.
Gotcha: paths contain indices, so changing pagination or arguments changes paths — never hardcode them in client logic.
Debugging: path locates the throw site in the graph, locations locates it in the query text — use both in trace overlays.
Testing tip: assert on path + extensions.code in integration tests; asserting on message strings is brittle.
Mutations follow the same path rules per field — but non-null root mutation fields escalate failures (see non-null propagation).

chapters.title: extensions.code: Machine-Readable Errors
points: extensions is a free-form object on each error for machine-readable data — message is for humans, extensions for programs.
De facto standard: extensions.code — Apollo Server popularized BAD_USER_INPUT, GRAPHQL_VALIDATION_FAILED, GRAPHQL_PARSE_FAILED, INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR.
Convention codes worth adopting: UNAUTHENTICATED, FORBIDDEN, NOT_FOUND, RATE_LIMITED, PAYMENT_REQUIRED.
Apollo maps thrown types: SyntaxError -> GRAPHQL_PARSE_FAILED, ValidationError -> GRAPHQL_VALIDATION_FAILED, anything unknown -> INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR.
Codes are an API contract: stable, documented, UPPERCASE — renaming a code is a breaking change like renaming a field.
Transport hints in extensions: code RATE_LIMITED plus retryAfter seconds lets clients back off correctly.
Structured validation payloads: extensions.invalidArgs [{field, issue}] or details — bind server errors to form fields.
Branch on extensions.code in clients — never regex the message; copy changes, codes do not.
Publish a code table like enum docs: code -> meaning -> expected client action.
Never leak debug data through extensions in production — sanitize extensions as aggressively as message.
HTTP mapping: GraphQL-over-HTTP guidance says application errors stay 200; only transport failures (malformed request, server down) get 4xx/5xx — some gateways map code -> status for legacy clients.
Antipattern: encoding machine info in the message (Error 403: user not found) — that is a code living in the wrong field.

chapters.title: Error Lifecycle Inside Resolvers
points: Two error phases: request errors (parse + validation, before any resolver runs) vs field errors (raised during execution).
Throwing in a resolver never crashes the request: the executor catches, converts to GraphQLError, appends to errors[], nulls the field.
GraphQLError constructor: new GraphQLError(message, { extensions, originalError }) — path and locations are auto-filled at execution time.
originalError preserves the root cause: chain it for server-side logging, strip it before sending to clients.
Pattern: define domain error classes (NotFound, Forbidden, RateLimited) carrying a code; a middleware maps class -> extensions.code.
Expected vs unexpected: throw curated GraphQLErrors for domain failures; let unknown exceptions surface as masked INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR.
Async resolvers: a rejected promise behaves exactly like a throw — the executor awaits and catches it.
Return-instead-of-throw: some teams model expected failures as union result types (comparisons chapter) and reserve errors[] for the unexpected.
Error volume: a resolver invoked per list item can emit thousands of errors — dedupe/aggregate in formatError.
Single choke point: shape all outgoing errors in formatError / didEncounterErrors hooks — never patch messages ad hoc across resolvers.
Attach requestId/userId in a server plugin before masking, so masked production errors stay traceable in logs.
Rule: never throw raw strings or plain objects — non-Error throws lose stack traces and break originalError chaining.

chapters.title: Non-Null Propagation: How One Error Nulls Everything
points: Core rule: if a non-null field (type T!) throws or resolves to null, the executor cannot place null there — it must propagate null to the parent.
Propagation continues: parent nullable -> parent becomes null (its other resolved fields are discarded too); parent also non-null -> null bubbles to the nearest nullable ancestor.
Worst case: an error under a chain of ! fields nulls the entire data object — one failing avatar can wipe the whole response.
errors[] still holds the original leaf error with the leaf path — nulling happens in data, the diagnosis stays in errors.
Fields are nullable by default in SDL: resilience is the default, non-null strictness is opt-in with !.
Use ! deliberately: fields whose null would make the parent meaningless (id: ID!, root fields returning objects).
Non-null root mutation fields give all-or-nothing semantics: a failure nulls data entirely — decide this consciously per mutation.
List gotcha: [Post!]! means a single bad post nulls the whole list; use [Post] (nullable items) for per-item failure isolation.
Trade-off: nullable = local failure + partial UI; non-null = stronger guarantees + bigger blast radius up the tree.
Audit nullability via introspection: every ! in the schema is a propagation edge — treat each as a failure-amplification point.
Null is not failure: a field can be legitimately null (missing data) with no error entry — check errors[] to distinguish absent vs failed.
Versioning: adding ! to an existing field is a breaking change — nullability is part of your public contract.

chapters.title: Masking Internal Errors
points: Threat: raw resolver exceptions leak stack traces, SQL, file paths, and third-party keys into errors[].message — free recon for attackers.
Golden rule: expected errors carry curated user-facing messages; unexpected errors are masked to a generic message and logged server-side.
Standard mask: message -> 'Internal server error', extensions.code -> INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, originalError logged, never shipped.
Correlation IDs: put a debug/correlationId in extensions so a user-reported failure maps to exactly one log line.
Fail closed with an allowlist: only instances of your public error classes pass through unmasked; everything else is masked.
Apollo Server 4 masks unexpected errors by default in production; includeStacktraceInErrorResponses and the debug flag control the rest.
Implement masking in formatError / didEncounterErrors — one choke point redacts message, strips originalError and stack.
Sanitize extensions too: a well-meaning details object can leak query params, internal IDs, or endpoint names.
Validation leak: 'Did you mean...' field suggestions reveal schema shape — disable them in production, as Apollo does.
Federation: downstream subgraph errors traverse the gateway — mask at the outermost edge, trust no passthrough.
Do not over-mask: blanket-masking NOT_FOUND or VALIDATION destroys UX — mask by error class, not everything.
CI test: throw a fake exception in a test resolver and assert the client sees only INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR — no stack, no originalError.

chapters.title: Client-Side Handling & Error Policies
points: Apollo Client error shape: error.graphQLErrors (array), error.networkError, error.clientErrors — handle all three, not just a try/catch.
Partial data still lands in the cache: data and errors arrive together — render what resolved, degrade the failed paths.
errorPolicy: none (default — errors reject the result, data dropped), ignore (errors dropped, data kept), all (data + graphQLErrors delivered together).
urql equivalent: the OperationResult carries error alongside data; CombinedError exposes graphQLErrors and networkError.
Retry policy by code: retry network errors with backoff, honor retryAfter for RATE_LIMITED, never retry VALIDATION or FORBIDDEN.
Map codes to UX: UNAUTHENTICATED -> login redirect, FORBIDDEN -> hide affordance, NOT_FOUND -> empty state, RATE_LIMITED -> countdown.
Path-driven recovery: match error.path to the component owning that fragment so only the broken subtree degrades.
Unpack structured validation: extensions.invalidArgs / details -> bind per-field form errors.
Classic bug: awaiting a query never rejects on field errors — failure arrives as a resolved response carrying errors[], so explicit checks are mandatory.
Two kinds of null: null with no error = data genuinely absent; null with a matching error = resolution failed — same shape, different UX.
Centralize mapping in one link/interceptor layer: codes -> typed app errors, so screens never parse raw GraphQL errors.
Dev vs prod: show path and locations in developer overlays; strip them from user-facing toasts.

chapters.title: GraphQL vs REST vs Unions: Trade-offs
points: vs REST: REST signals per-endpoint status codes (200/404/500) — coarse and all-or-nothing; GraphQL reports per-field in-band with transport 200.
GraphQL-over-HTTP guidance: application failures = 200 + errors[]; only transport-level failures (malformed request, server down) deserve 4xx/5xx.
Alternative pattern: result unions (type UserResult = User | NotFoundError | PermissionError) make failures visible in the schema and force exhaustive handling.
Union trade-off: compile-time safety vs verbosity — every query must inline fragments (... on NotFoundError) and the schema grows per failure mode.
errors[] trade-off: uniform and spec-blessed but invisible to the type system — clients can silently ignore them.
Hybrid convention used by strong APIs: expected domain failures -> union types; unexpected/infra failures -> masked errors[].
vs gRPC: 16 canonical gRPC status codes per call vs free-form extensions.code per API — standardization vs domain expressiveness.
Payload bloat: a list with many failing items can emit more error objects than data — cap, dedupe, or aggregate.
Caching: only data is cacheable, errors are not — error-heavy designs push recovery complexity onto every client.
Observability: partial responses make request success ambiguous — track error rate per path and code, not per request.
Masking tension: hiding internals protects you and blinds you — solve with correlationId plus full server-side detail.
Where errors[] shines: heterogeneous or federated graphs where independent sources fail independently — per-node failure is the norm.

chapters.title: Common Mistakes & Cheat Sheet
points: Mistake 1: throwing raw Error with internal messages in production — wrap expected failures in coded GraphQLErrors, mask the rest.
Mistake 2: sprinkling ! everywhere for safety — every non-null is a propagation edge; one failure can null the whole response.
Mistake 3: if (errors) return — discarding valid partial data; render what resolved, degrade the failed paths.
Mistake 4: branching on message strings or regex — extensions.code is the contract, message is human copy.
Mistake 5: leaking stack traces via originalError serialization or a debug extensions field.
Mistake 6: infinite retry loops on non-retryable codes like VALIDATION or FORBIDDEN.
Mistake 7: treating null as failure (or ignoring failed nulls) — join against errors[].path before deciding UX.
Mistake 8: unbounded error arrays from hot list resolvers — dedupe and cap in formatError.
Mistake 9: masking in subgraphs but trusting the gateway passthrough — mask at the outermost edge.
Cheat sheet: response = data? + errors[]; each error = message + locations + path + extensions.code.
Cheat sheet: null + no error = absent; null + error = failed; ! = propagation edge; request errors carry no path.
Final checklist: nullable by default, curate expected errors, mask unexpected, code in extensions, always render partial data, retry only retryable codes.
